q: Which sentence for a front-desk sign uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: There was several reasons that the appointment had to be moved.
Here is the signed consent forms for the two new patients.
There is two forms that every new patient must sign at check-in.
On the counter sit two charts that still need a provider's signature.
w: When a sentence is inverted, find the subject after the verb. "Charts" is the subject of "sit," and both are plural, so "On the counter sit two charts" is correct.

n.0: The subject is "reasons" (plural), which comes after the verb, so it must be "There were."
n.1: The subject that follows the verb is "forms" (plural), so it must be "Here are the signed consent forms."
n.2: In a "there" sentence the subject follows the verb. The subject is "forms" (plural), so it must be "There are."

q: Which sentence about nursing school admissions uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: The news about the new admission deadlines was posted on Monday.
The number of applicants to the program have doubled since 2020.
A number of applicants has asked whether the essay is required.
Twenty dollars are the fee that each applicant pays to submit a form.
w: "News" ends in -s but is singular, so it takes "was." Remember: "the number of" is singular, "a number of" is plural, and a sum of money is singular.

n.1: "The number of" is singular (it names one figure), so the verb must be "has doubled."
n.2: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb: "A number of applicants have asked."
n.3: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular: "Twenty dollars is the fee."

q: Which sentence about the crash-cart check uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither the students nor the nurse are checking the crash cart today.
The nurse, along with two students, are checking the crash cart.
The nurse, as well as two students, is checking the crash cart.
The nurse and two students, with the instructor, is checking the cart.
w: Phrases such as "as well as," "along with" and "together with" do not make a subject plural. The subject is "nurse," so the verb is "is."

n.0: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "nurse," which is singular, so it must be "is."
n.1: "Along with two students" is an intervening phrase, not part of the subject. The subject "nurse" is singular, so the verb must be "is."
n.3: "The nurse and two students" is a compound subject joined by "and," which is plural, so the verb must be "are."

q: Which revision corrects the agreement error? "The quality of the images from the older scanners have improved since the software update."
o: Change "have improved" to "were improved."
Change "have improved" to "has improved."
Change "scanners" to "scanner."
Change "images" to "image."
w: The subject is "quality" (singular). "Of the images from the older scanners" is an intervening phrase, so the verb must be singular: "has improved."

n.0: "Were" is still plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject "quality," and it changes the meaning to passive.
n.2: "Scanners" is inside a prepositional phrase and is not the subject; the plural verb "have" would still disagree with "quality."
n.3: "Images" is also inside a prepositional phrase; the true subject "quality" still needs "has," so the error remains.

q: Which sentence from an end-of-day inventory report uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Some of the patients in the waiting room is asking about the delay.
Most of the hand sanitizer in the supply room has been used this week.
All of the lab samples from this morning has been labeled and stored.
Half of the coffee in the break room were gone by the end of the night shift.
w: All, some, most and fractions such as half take their number from the noun after "of." "Sanitizer" is uncountable, so "Most of the hand sanitizer ... has been used" is correct.

n.0: "Some" refers to "patients" (plural) here, so the verb must be "are asking."
n.2: "All" takes its number from the noun after "of." "Samples" is plural, so the verb must be "have been labeled."
n.3: "Half" agrees with the noun after "of." "Coffee" is uncountable, so the verb must be singular: "was gone."

q: Which sentence from a hospital welcome packet contains an error in subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither of the two applicants has submitted a transcript yet.
The bag of IV fluid hanging by the bed is due to be replaced.
There are a clipboard and two pens at the front desk for visitors.
Each of the patients on the third floor have a call button.
w: "Each" is always singular, so the verb must be "has": "Each of the patients on the third floor has a call button." The plural "patients" sits inside a prepositional phrase.

n.0: This sentence is correct: "neither" used as a pronoun is singular, so "has submitted" agrees.
n.1: This sentence is correct: the subject "bag" is singular and takes "is"; "of IV fluid hanging by the bed" does not change it.
n.2: This sentence is correct: the subject after the verb is compound ("a clipboard and two pens"), so the plural "are" agrees.

q: Which sentence about the hospital unit contains a subject-verb agreement error?
o: The aides, as well as the nurse, were praised by the family.
Each of the rooms on the unit has its own thermostat.
Six hours is a long time to wait for test results.
The supply of masks and gowns are running low this week.
w: The subject is "supply," which is singular, so the verb must be "is running." "Of masks and gowns" is an intervening prepositional phrase.

n.0: This sentence is correct: "as well as the nurse" does not change the plural subject "aides," so "were" agrees.
n.1: This sentence is correct: "Each" is singular, so "has" agrees, and "its" matches "each."
n.2: This sentence is correct: an amount of time treated as one block is singular, so "Six hours is" agrees.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The results of the patient's blood test ___ ready for the cardiologist to review."
o: is
are
was
has been
w: The subject is "results," which is plural, so the verb is "are." "Of the patient's blood test" is an intervening prepositional phrase.

n.0: "Is" agrees with "test," the object of the preposition, not with the plural subject "results."
n.2: "Was" is singular; the plural subject "results" needs "are" (or "were").
n.3: "Has been" is singular; the plural subject "results" would need "have been."

q: Which sentence about the clinic staff uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Each of the new nurses have completed the orientation module.
Neither the manager nor the nurses was told about the fire drill.
The aides, together with the nurse, is checking the supply carts.
The staff meets in the conference room every Monday morning.
w: "Staff" is a collective noun acting as one unit, so in US English it takes the singular verb "meets."

n.0: "Each" is singular, so the verb must be "has completed"; "nurses" sits in a prepositional phrase.
n.1: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "nurses," so it must be "were told."
n.2: "Together with the nurse" does not change the subject; "aides" is plural, so the verb must be "are checking."

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "Several of the charts on the desk needs a signature before the patients go home."
o: go
charts
needs
Several
w: "Several" is an indefinite pronoun that is always plural, so the verb must be "need": "Several of the charts ... need a signature."

n.0: "Go" agrees with the plural subject "patients" in the clause "before the patients go home."
n.1: "Charts" is correctly plural as the object of "of"; it is not the subject of the verb.
n.3: "Several" is a correct plural subject here; the error is the singular verb that follows it.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "Either the pharmacist or the two technicians ___ the refill requests each afternoon."
o: checks
has checked
is checking
check
w: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject. "Technicians" is nearer and plural, so the verb is "check."

n.0: "Checks" agrees with "pharmacist," the farther subject; the nearer subject "technicians" is plural.
n.1: "Has checked" is singular and agrees with the farther subject, "pharmacist."
n.2: "Is checking" is singular; the nearer subject "technicians" needs "are checking."

q: Which sentence about the clinic's fees uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Forty dollars is the usual copay for a specialist visit.
The number of unpaid bills have dropped since January.
The news from the billing office were better than expected.
A number of patients has asked about the new payment plan.
w: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular, so "Forty dollars is the usual copay" is correct.

n.1: "The number of" names one figure and is singular, so the verb must be "has dropped."
n.2: "News" ends in -s but is singular, so the verb must be "was."
n.3: "A number of" means "several" and is plural, so the verb must be "have asked."

q: Which verb correctly completes the question? "Where ___ the extra boxes of gloves that arrived this morning stored?"
o: was
has been
is
are
w: In a question the subject follows the verb. The subject is "boxes," which is plural, so the verb is "are."

n.0: "Was" is singular; the plural subject "boxes" needs "are" (or "were").
n.1: "Has been" is singular; the plural subject "boxes" would need "have been."
n.2: "Is" is singular, but the subject "boxes" is plural; "gloves" is only the object of "of."

q: Which sentence with a compound subject uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither the patient nor his daughters remembers the dosage.
The nurse and the respiratory therapist is reviewing the plan.
Macaroni and cheese is the side dish on every lunch tray today.
Either the aides or the charge nurse are bringing the blankets.
w: "Macaroni and cheese" names one dish, a single unit, so it takes the singular verb "is."

n.0: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "daughters," so it must be "remember."
n.1: Two subjects joined by "and" are plural, so the verb must be "are reviewing."
n.3: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "charge nurse," so it must be "is bringing."

q: Which revision corrects the agreement error in "Here's the forms that the new patient needs to sign before the exam"?
o: Here are the forms that the new patient needs to sign before the exam.
Here's the forms that the new patient need to sign before the exam.
Here are the forms that the new patient need to sign before the exam.
Here is the forms that the new patient needs to sign before the exam.
w: The subject "forms" follows the verb and is plural, so "Here are" is needed. Inside the clause, "patient" is singular, so "needs" stays.

n.1: "Here's" is still "here is" with the plural "forms," and "patient need" adds a second agreement error.
n.2: "Here are" is fixed, but "the new patient need" breaks agreement; a singular subject takes "needs."
n.3: "Here is" is singular, but the subject that follows it, "forms," is plural.

q: Which verb correctly completes the sentence? "The main cause of the delays ___ the two broken elevators."
o: are
have been
were
is
w: The verb agrees with the subject, "cause," which is singular, not with the complement "elevators" that follows the verb.

n.0: "Are" agrees with "delays" or "elevators," but the subject is the singular "cause."
n.1: "Have been" is plural; the singular subject "cause" would need "has been."
n.2: "Were" is plural; the singular subject "cause" needs "is" (or "was").

q: Which sentence from a lab safety notice uses a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent?
o: Each of the vials must be inspected for cracks before it is used.
The lab and the pharmacy will extend its hours in December.
If a student wants to pass, you have to practice every day.
All of the incubators must have its filters changed every month.
w: "Each" is singular, and a vial is a thing, so the singular pronoun "it" agrees in number and person.

n.1: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their hours."
n.2: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you"); keep the same person throughout.
n.3: "All" refers to "incubators" (plural) here, so the pronoun must be plural: "their filters."

q: Which sentence contains a shift in pronoun person that should be corrected?
o: When one reads a drug label, you should check the expiration date first.
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember it.
We volunteers should bring our badges to every shift this month.
Applicants should check their email often, since the school sends updates there.
w: "One" is third person, but "you" is second person. Keep one point of view: "When you read a drug label, you should..."

n.1: This sentence stays in second person throughout ("you" and the implied "you" of "take").
n.2: This sentence stays in first person plural: "we" and "our."
n.3: This sentence is consistent: "applicants" and "their" are both third person plural.

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The nursing students must submit ___ immunization records before the first clinical day."
o: her
your
their
they're
w: The antecedent "students" is plural and third person, so the plural possessive "their" agrees.

n.0: "Her" is singular, but the antecedent "students" is plural.
n.1: "Your" is second person; the antecedent "students" is third person, so this is a shift.
n.3: "They're" means "they are"; the sentence needs a possessive pronoun.

q: Which sentence about the hospital uses a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent?
o: Dr. Reyes and Dr. Moss presented her findings to the board.
The two pharmacies changed its hours for the holiday.
The ethics committee announced its decision on Monday.
If a patient feels dizzy, you should sit down right away.
w: The committee acts as one body, so the singular "its" agrees with it.

n.0: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their findings."
n.1: "Pharmacies" is plural, so the pronoun must be "their hours."
n.3: The sentence shifts from third person ("a patient") to second person ("you").

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Neither Mr. Ruiz nor the aides remembered to bring ___ badges to the meeting."
o: their
they're
there
his
w: With "neither...nor," the pronoun agrees with the nearer antecedent. "Aides" is nearer and plural, so "their" is correct.

n.1: "They're" means "they are"; the sentence needs a possessive pronoun before "badges."
n.2: "There" names a place; the sentence needs the possessive pronoun "their."
n.3: "His" agrees with "Mr. Ruiz," the farther antecedent; the nearer one, "aides," is plural.

q: Which revision corrects the pronoun shift in "When a nurse starts on a new unit, you should ask for a tour"?
o: When nurses start on a new unit, she should ask for a tour.
When nurses start on a new unit, they should ask for a tour.
When nurses start on a new unit, you should ask for a tour.
When a nurse starts on a new unit, we should ask for a tour.
w: "Nurses" (third person plural) is matched by "they" (third person plural), so person and number agree.

n.0: "She" is singular, but the antecedent "nurses" is plural.
n.2: This still shifts from third person ("nurses") to second person ("you").
n.3: This shifts from third person ("a nurse") to first person ("we").

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "The clinic will move ___ main entrance to Oak Street next month."
o: its'
they're
it's
its
w: The clinic is one thing, so it takes the singular possessive pronoun "its," which has no apostrophe.

n.0: "Its'" is not a word; possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.
n.1: "They're" means "they are" and is plural; the clinic needs the possessive "its."
n.2: "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; "move it is main entrance" makes no sense.

q: Which sentence about clinic equipment uses a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent?
o: The binders on the top shelf have lost their colored labels.
The new infusion pump arrived, but they are missing a cord.
Each of the monitors on the unit needs their screen cleaned.
The scale and the monitor in Room 2 need its batteries replaced.
w: "Binders" is plural, so the plural pronoun "their" agrees with it.

n.1: "Pump" is singular, so the pronoun must be "it is missing a cord."
n.2: "Each" is singular and refers to things, so the pronoun must be "its screen."
n.3: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their batteries."

q: Which sentence about practice tests keeps the same point of view?
o: If applicants want higher scores, one should take timed practice tests.
If applicants want higher scores, they should take timed practice tests.
If applicants want higher scores, you should take timed practice tests.
If an applicant wants higher scores, we should take timed practice tests.
w: "Applicants" is third person plural, so the pronoun "they" keeps the same person and number.

n.0: "One" is singular and generic, so it no longer refers to the plural "applicants."
n.2: "You" is second person, so it shifts away from the third person "applicants."
n.3: "We" is first person, so it shifts away from the third person "an applicant."

q: Which sentence from a unit report contains a pronoun-antecedent agreement error?
o: The lab coats were returned, but it had not been washed.
The volunteers signed in and picked up their name tags.
The twins brought their own snacks to the checkup.
Mercy Hospital posted its new visiting hours online.
w: "Coats" is plural, so the pronoun must be plural: "they had not been washed."

n.1: This sentence is correct: "volunteers" is plural and "their" is plural.
n.2: This sentence is correct: "twins" is plural and "their" is plural.
n.3: This sentence is correct: the hospital is one organization, so "its" agrees.

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "The pharmacy and the lab will extend it's hours during the flu season."
o: it's
during
will
pharmacy
w: The antecedent "the pharmacy and the lab" is plural, so the pronoun must be "their." "It's" also means "it is," not a possessive.

n.1: "During" is a correct preposition before "the flu season."
n.2: "Will extend" is a correct future verb for the plural subject.
n.3: "Pharmacy" is correct as part of the compound subject.

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Several of the cardiac monitors lost ___ signal during the storm last night."
o: its
it's
their
there
w: "Several" is always plural, so the plural possessive "their" agrees with it.

n.0: "Its" is singular, but "several" is plural.
n.1: "It's" means "it is" and is singular; the sentence needs a plural possessive.
n.3: "There" names a place; the sentence needs the possessive pronoun "their."

q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "As nursing applicants, we know that ___ scores on the HESI A2 matter."
o: us
their
our
your
w: The antecedent "we" is first person plural, so the possessive must be "our."

n.0: "Us" is an objective pronoun, not a possessive, so it cannot come before "scores."
n.1: "Their" is third person; it shifts away from the first person "we."
n.3: "Your" is second person; it shifts away from the first person "we."

q: Which word group from a staff training packet is a complete sentence?
o: The nurse who works nights and trains the new aides.
The nurse who works nights trained the new aide.
Running to the clinic before the nurse's night shift.
Because the nurse who works nights trained the aide.
w: "The nurse ... trained the new aide" has a subject (nurse), a main verb (trained) and a complete thought; "who works nights" is a relative clause inside it.

n.0: The verbs "works" and "trains" both belong to the relative clause beginning with "who", so "The nurse" has no main verb: a fragment.
n.2: This is a participial phrase with no subject and no main verb.
n.3: "Because" makes the whole word group a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.

q: Which sentence about a missed appointment is a comma splice?
o: The bus was late, we missed the appointment.
Because the bus was late, we missed the appointment.
The bus was late; we missed the appointment.
The bus was late, so we missed the appointment.
w: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma. "The bus was late" and "we missed the appointment" can each stand alone.

n.1: The first clause is dependent (Because ...), so a comma after it is correct.
n.2: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
n.3: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction "so" correctly joins two independent clauses.

q: Which revision corrects the run-on sentence "The power went out the generator started within seconds"?
o: The power went out and, the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, however the generator started within seconds.
The power went out, and the generator started within seconds.
w: A comma followed by a coordinating conjunction (and) correctly joins two independent clauses.

n.0: The comma must come before the conjunction, not after it.
n.1: Adding only a comma turns the run-on into a comma splice.
n.2: "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma before it still leaves a comma splice.

q: Which revision corrects the comma splice in "The patient felt dizzy, however, she refused to sit down"?
o: The patient felt dizzy; however, she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy however, she refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy, she, however, refused to sit down.
The patient felt dizzy, however she refused to sit down.
w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.

n.1: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.
n.2: Moving "however" inside the second clause still leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma.
n.3: A comma before "however" still joins two independent clauses with only a comma: a comma splice.

q: Which revision correctly fixes the fragment? "Because the patient was allergic to penicillin. The doctor prescribed a different antibiotic."
o: Because the patient was allergic to penicillin; the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
The patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin the doctor, prescribed a different antibiotic.
Because the patient was allergic to penicillin, the doctor prescribed a different antibiotic.
w: The dependent clause (Because ... penicillin) is attached to the independent clause with a comma, giving a correct complex sentence.

n.0: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; the first part is a dependent clause.
n.1: Removing "Because" leaves two independent clauses joined by only a comma: a comma splice.
n.2: The comma is misplaced: it separates the subject (the doctor) from its verb, and the comma after the introductory clause is missing.

q: Which sentence from a weekly staffing update is structured correctly?
o: The clinic was short-staffed on Friday. Because several walk-ins arrived before nine.
Although the clinic was short-staffed, the nurses kept every visit on schedule.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday, several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
The clinic was short-staffed on Friday several walk-in patients arrived before nine.
w: A dependent clause (Although the clinic was short-staffed) followed by a comma and an independent clause is a correct complex sentence.

n.0: The second word group begins with "Because" and has no independent clause, so it is a fragment.
n.2: Two independent clauses joined by only a comma form a comma splice.
n.3: Two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction form a run-on (fused) sentence.

q: Which word group from a student's clinical notes is a fragment?
o: She hoped to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
Hoping to finish her charting before the end of the shift.
Hoping to finish, she charted before the end of the shift.
Finish your charting before the end of the shift.
w: Two steps: "Hoping" is a participle, not a main verb, and the word group has no subject, so it cannot stand alone.

n.0: This has a subject (She) and a main verb (hoped), so it is complete.
n.2: The participial phrase is attached to the independent clause "she charted ...", so it is complete.
n.3: This is an imperative sentence; its subject "you" is understood, so it is complete.

q: Which revision corrects the comma splice "The roads were icy, the clinic opened late" and shows cause and effect?
o: The roads were icy, the clinic, therefore, opened late.
Because the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
Although the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
The roads were icy, but the clinic opened late.
w: Two steps: subordinating one clause fixes the splice, and "Because" signals cause and effect.

n.0: The two independent clauses are still joined by only a comma, so the splice remains.
n.2: "Although" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.
n.3: "But" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.

q: Which line from a patient instruction sheet is a complete sentence?
o: Please sign the consent form before the procedure.
Signing the consent form before the procedure.
Since the consent form was signed before the procedure.
The consent form that was signed before the procedure.
w: An imperative sentence is complete even though its subject (you) is not stated: "[You] Please sign the consent form."

n.1: This is a gerund phrase with no main verb.
n.2: "Since" makes this a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.3: "That was signed ..." is a relative clause describing the form; the subject "The consent form" has no main verb.

q: Which revision corrects the faulty predication in "Hypoglycemia is when the blood glucose level drops too low"?
o: Hypoglycemia is where the blood glucose level drops too low.
Hypoglycemia, is a condition in which the blood glucose level drops too low.
Hypoglycemia is a condition in which the blood glucose level drops too low.
Hypoglycemia is a condition in which the blood glucose level drop too low.
w: After a linking verb such as "is," the subject must be renamed by a noun phrase. "A condition in which..." renames hypoglycemia; "is when" (a time) and "is where" (a place) do not, so they are faulty predication.

n.0: "Is where" is still faulty predication: hypoglycemia is a condition, not a place.
n.1: The predication is fixed, but the comma now separates the subject (Hypoglycemia) from its verb (is).
n.3: The predication is fixed, but the singular subject "level" needs the singular verb "drops," not "drop."

q: Which sentence from a clinical narrative is free of a dangling modifier?
o: Walking into the clinic, the crowd in the lobby surprised her.
Walking into the clinic, it was clear that the lobby was full.
Walking into the clinic, Rosa saw that the lobby was crowded.
Walking into the clinic, the lobby looked crowded to Rosa.
w: An introductory participial phrase must be followed by the person or thing doing the action. Rosa was walking into the clinic, so "Rosa" must come right after the comma.

n.0: The subject after the phrase is "the crowd," so the sentence says the crowd was walking into the clinic.
n.1: "It" cannot do the walking; the person who walked in never appears as the subject.
n.3: The phrase "Walking into the clinic" is followed by "the lobby," so the sentence says the lobby was walking.

q: Of the network's four sites, the downtown clinic is the one that schedules two nurses on weekends. Which sentence states this most clearly?
o: The downtown clinic only schedules two nurses on weekends.
The downtown clinic schedules only two nurses on weekends.
Only the downtown clinic schedules two nurses on weekends.
The downtown clinic schedules two nurses only on weekends.
w: A limiting word such as only, just, nearly or almost goes directly before the word it limits. The point is that no other site does this, so "only" must come before "the downtown clinic."

n.0: Placed before the verb, "only" limits what the clinic does (or, loosely, the number); it never says that no other site does it.
n.1: Placed before "two nurses," "only" limits the number of nurses, not which site schedules them.
n.3: Placed before "on weekends," "only" limits the days: nurses are scheduled on weekends and not on weekdays.

q: The flyers have large print. Which sentence places the modifier "with large print" correctly?
o: The volunteer handed out flyers to the families with large print.
The volunteer handed out flyers with large print to the families.
The volunteer with large print handed out flyers to the families.
With large print, the volunteer handed out flyers to the families.
w: A modifier belongs next to the word it describes. The large print is on the flyers, so the phrase must follow "flyers."

n.0: Placed after "families," the phrase seems to describe the families, not the flyers.
n.2: Placed after "volunteer," the phrase describes the volunteer instead of the flyers.
n.3: Placed at the start, the phrase seems to describe the volunteer, who is not printed.

q: Which revision corrects the dangling modifier in "After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered"?
o: After reviewing the lab results, the doctor ordered a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's order called for a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered by the doctor.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's decision was to order a new medication.
w: The person who reviewed the results (the doctor) must be the subject right after the introductory phrase.

n.1: The subject after the comma is "order," so the sentence says the order reviewed the results; the doctor must be the subject.
n.2: The subject after the comma is still "a new medication," so the sentence still says the medication reviewed the results.
n.3: The subject after the comma is "decision," and a decision cannot review lab results; "doctor's" is only a possessive.

q: Which sentence about training for new aides uses parallel structure?
o: New aides learn to take vital signs, record intake, and reposition patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, to record intake, and how to reposition patients.
New aides learn taking vital signs, to record intake, and repositioning patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, recording intake, and to reposition patients.
w: Items in a series must share one grammatical form. After "learn to," the three base verbs (take, record, reposition) are parallel.

n.1: The third item switches from an infinitive ("to record") to a "how to" phrase, so the list is not parallel.
n.2: The list mixes gerunds ("taking," "repositioning") with an infinitive ("to record").
n.3: "Recording" is a gerund placed between two infinitives, which breaks the parallel pattern.

q: Which sentence from a college brochure uses "not only...but also" correctly?
o: The program not only trains nurses but also places them in local clinics.
The program not only trains nurses but also it places them in local clinics.
Not only does the program train nurses but also places them in local clinics.
The program trains not only nurses but also places them in local clinics.
w: Correlative pairs must be followed by matching elements. Here each part is followed by a verb phrase: "not only trains ... but also places."

n.1: "But also" is followed by a full clause ("it places"), while "not only" is followed by a verb; the two parts do not match.
n.2: "Not only" introduces an inverted clause, but "but also" introduces a bare verb phrase, so the pair is not parallel.
n.3: "Not only" precedes a noun ("nurses") but "but also" precedes a verb ("places"); each part needs the same form.

q: Which sentence comparing two urgent care centers makes a logical, parallel comparison?
o: Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than those at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than the staff at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than Eastside Clinic is.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than at Eastside Clinic's.
w: A comparison must set like things side by side: wait times at one clinic versus wait times ("those") at the other.

n.1: This compares wait times to the staff, two unlike things; the comparison needs "those at Eastside Clinic."
n.2: This still compares wait times (plural) with a clinic (singular), which is illogical.
n.3: The possessive "Eastside Clinic's" leaves the noun it owns unstated, so the comparison is garbled.

q: Which revision corrects the faulty parallelism in "The new policy is meant to reduce wait times, improving patient satisfaction, and to lower costs"?
o: Change "to reduce" to "reducing."
Change "to lower" to "lowering."
Delete the word "and" before "to lower."
Change "improving" to "to improve."
w: Two of the three items are infinitives (to reduce, to lower). Changing "improving" to "to improve" makes all three match.

n.0: This leaves "to lower" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.1: This leaves "to reduce" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.2: Removing "and" does not change the forms of the items and also leaves the series without its conjunction.

q: Which sentence from a student handbook draft has parallel structure?
o: The applicant was praised for her punctuality, her empathy, and for being skilled.
The checklist asks staff to wash hands, wear gloves, and dispose of sharps safely.
Volunteers may greet visitors, deliver flowers, or they can read to patients.
The course teaches students how to splint a fracture and controlling bleeding.
w: All three items after "to" are base verbs (wash, wear, dispose), so the series is parallel.

n.0: Two nouns ("her punctuality," "her empathy") are followed by a gerund phrase with a repeated "for"; it should be "and her clinical skill."
n.2: The first two items are verb phrases, but the third is a full clause ("they can read"); it should be "or read to patients."
n.3: "How to splint" is paired with the gerund "controlling"; it should be "how to splint a fracture and control bleeding."

q: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence? "All visitors must ___ the hospital's mask policy."
o: comply to
comply with
comply by
comply for
w: The standard idiom is "comply with" a rule or policy.

n.0: "Comply to" is a nonstandard idiom; the verb takes "with."
n.2: "By" belongs to a different idiom, "abide by"; "comply" takes "with."
n.3: "Comply for" is not a standard idiom.

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "The appointment is scheduled ___ Tuesday ___ 9:30 a.m."
o: in / at
at / on
on / in
on / at
w: Use "on" with days and dates and "at" with a clock time: "on Tuesday at 9:30 a.m."

n.0: "In" is for months, years and parts of the day, not a named day.
n.1: This reverses the pair: days take "on" and clock times take "at."
n.2: "On Tuesday" is right, but a clock time takes "at," not "in."

q: Which sentence from a patient's allergy record uses prepositions correctly?
o: The patient is allergic to penicillin and sensitive to latex.
The patient is allergic with penicillin and sensitive to latex.
The patient is allergic of penicillin and sensitive to latex.
The patient is allergic to penicillin and sensitive with latex.
w: The standard idioms are "allergic to" and "sensitive to."

n.1: "Allergic with" is nonstandard; the idiom is "allergic to."
n.2: "Allergic of" is nonstandard; the idiom is "allergic to."
n.3: "Sensitive with" is nonstandard; the idiom is "sensitive to."

q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "Ms. Ortiz walked ___ the exam room and waited ___ the room for the doctor."
o: in / at
in / into
into / in
into / into
w: "Into" shows movement to the inside (walked into the room); "in" shows location (waited in the room).

n.0: Walking to the inside of a room needs "into," and an enclosed room takes "in," not "at."
n.1: This reverses the pair: walking is movement (into), and waiting is location (in).
n.3: Waiting is not movement, so the second blank needs "in."

q: Which sentence about a patient's medications uses "beside" or "besides" correctly?
o: Besides the bed, a small table held the patient's water pitcher.
Beside the morning dose, the patient needs an evening tablet.
The call light hangs besides the bed, within easy reach.
Besides the morning dose, the patient needs an evening tablet.
w: "Besides" means "in addition to": in addition to the morning dose, the patient needs an evening tablet.

n.0: The table is next to the bed, so the word must be "beside."
n.1: The meaning is "in addition to," so the word must be "besides."
n.2: The call light is next to the bed, so the word must be "beside."

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Mr. Diaz has been a patient on the cardiac unit ___ Monday."
o: from
for
until
since
w: "Since" marks the starting point of a period that continues to now: since Monday.

n.0: "From" needs an end point (from Monday until Friday) and does not fit "has been."
n.1: "For" is used with a length of time (for three days), not a starting day.
n.2: "Until" marks an end point (until Monday), but "has been" needs the starting point.

q: Which sentence about unit routines uses a standard idiom?
o: The new aide is capable to lift patients with the mechanical lift.
The new sign-in policy is similar with the one used at Mercy.
Each nurse is responsible for checking the crash cart every shift.
The trauma kit consists in gauze, tape, and two pairs of gloves.
w: "Responsible for" is the standard idiom.

n.0: The idiom is "capable of" plus an -ing form: "capable of lifting."
n.1: The idiom is "similar to," not "similar with."
n.3: To list what something is made of, the idiom is "consists of."

q: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence? "I am writing ___ your request for a copy of your records."
o: in regard of
in regards to
in regard to
in regards of
w: The standard phrase is "in regard to" (or "with regard to"), with no s on "regard."

n.0: "In regard of" uses the wrong preposition; the phrase ends with "to."
n.1: "In regards to" is a nonstandard form; "regard" takes no s in this phrase.
n.3: "In regards of" adds an s and uses the wrong preposition.

q: Which sentence about flu season uses prepositions of time correctly?
o: Flu shots start on October and end in early March.
Flu shots start in October and end in early March.
Flu shots start at October and end on early March.
Flu shots start in October and end at early March.
w: Months and parts of a month take "in": in October, in early March.

n.0: "On" is for days and dates; a month takes "in."
n.2: "At" is for clock times and "on" for days; months take "in."
n.3: "At" is for clock times; "early March" is part of a month and takes "in."

q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Patients should abstain ___ food and drink for eight hours before the test."
o: from
of
to
with
w: The standard idiom is "abstain from."

n.1: "Abstain of" is nonstandard; the verb takes "from."
n.2: "Abstain to" is nonstandard; the verb takes "from."
n.3: "Abstain with" is nonstandard; the verb takes "from."

q: Which sentence about the crash cart contains an unnecessary preposition?
o: Where did you put the crash cart?
Where is the crash cart at right now?
The crash cart is next to the nurses' station.
Which room is the crash cart in?
w: "Where" already means "at what place," so the "at" adds nothing: "Where is the crash cart right now?"

n.0: This question is correct and has no extra preposition.
n.2: "Next to" is needed to show location, so it is not extra.
n.3: "In" is needed to complete "in which room"; ending a sentence with a preposition is standard.

q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "Mina has been interested on pediatric nursing since her first clinical rotation."
o: interested
her
since
on
w: The standard idiom is "interested in," so "on" should be "in."

n.0: "Interested" is the correct adjective; the error is the preposition after it.
n.1: "Her" correctly refers to Mina.
n.2: "Since" correctly marks the starting point, "her first clinical rotation."

q: Which sentence about the supply delivery uses prepositions of place correctly?
o: The boxes are on the storage room, at the top shelf.
The boxes are in the storage room, at the top shelf.
The boxes are at the storage room, in the top shelf.
The boxes are in the storage room, on the top shelf.
w: Use "in" for an enclosed space (in the storage room) and "on" for a surface (on the top shelf).

n.0: A room is an enclosed space (in), and a shelf is a surface (on); both are swapped.
n.1: "In the storage room" is right, but a shelf is a surface and takes "on."
n.2: A room takes "in," not "at," and a shelf takes "on," not "in."

q: Which sentence from a shift report is punctuated correctly?
o: The nurse, checked the patient's chart and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
w: When a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction: "chart, and the doctor".

n.0: A comma must not separate a subject (The nurse) from its verb (checked), and the comma before "and" is missing.
n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "and" is needed.
n.3: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.

q: Which sentence from an aide's charting note is punctuated correctly?
o: The aide measured the patient's blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide measured the patient's blood pressure, and recorded it in the chart.
The aide, measured the patient's blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
The aide measured the patient's, blood pressure and recorded it in the chart.
w: This is one subject (The aide) with a compound predicate (measured ... and recorded). With no second subject, there is no second independent clause, so no comma goes before "and".

n.1: A comma before "and" is used when it joins two independent clauses; here "recorded it" has no subject of its own.
n.2: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb.
n.3: A comma must not split a possessive from the noun it modifies.

q: Which sentence from a lab supervisor's note is punctuated correctly?
o: Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon the samples were stored until Monday.
Because, the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples were stored until Monday.
Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples were stored until Monday.
Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon, the samples, were stored until Monday.
w: A long introductory dependent clause (Because the hematology lab closed early on Friday afternoon) is followed by a comma before the main clause.

n.0: The comma after the long introductory dependent clause is missing, so the reader runs "afternoon the samples" together.
n.1: No comma follows the subordinating conjunction "Because".
n.3: A comma must not separate the subject (the samples) from its verb (were stored).

q: Which sentence introducing the surgeon on call is punctuated correctly?
o: Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight, will review the scans.
Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight will review the scans.
Dr. Patel, the surgeon on call tonight, will review, the scans.
Dr. Patel the surgeon on call tonight, will review the scans.
w: A nonessential appositive that renames a proper noun is set off by a pair of commas, one before it and one after it.

n.1: The closing comma after "tonight" is missing; a nonessential element needs commas on both sides.
n.2: A comma must not separate the verb (will review) from its object (the scans).
n.3: The opening comma after "Dr. Patel" is missing.

q: A unit has twelve patients, and only one of them fell yesterday. Which sentence correctly identifies that particular patient?
o: The patient who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday needs an X-ray before noon.
The patient, who fell yesterday, needs an X-ray before noon.
w: Two steps: with twelve patients, "who fell yesterday" is essential (restrictive) because it identifies which patient. Essential clauses take no commas.

n.1: A comma must not separate the subject from its verb (needs).
n.2: A single comma after "patient" opens an aside that is never closed.
n.3: Commas would mark the clause as nonessential, as if there were only one patient; here it is needed to identify the patient.

q: Which sentence about Riverside Clinic is punctuated correctly?
o: Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic, which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020, now offers evening hours.
Riverside Clinic which opened in 2020 now offers evening hours.
w: A proper noun is already identified, so the clause "which opened in 2020" is nonessential and needs a pair of commas.

n.1: The closing comma after "2020" is missing.
n.2: The opening comma after "Riverside Clinic" is missing.
n.3: A nonessential clause after a proper noun must be set off with commas.

q: Which sentence from a nurse's journal punctuates the adjectives correctly?
o: It was a long tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring, shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy, emergency room.
w: "Long" and "tiring" are coordinate adjectives (they could be joined by "and"), so a comma separates them. "Emergency room" is a compound noun, so "busy" takes no comma.

n.0: Coordinate adjectives that each describe the noun separately are separated by a comma: "long, tiring".
n.1: No comma goes between the last adjective and the noun it modifies.
n.3: "Emergency" is part of the noun "emergency room", so no comma follows "busy".

q: Which sentence about the new hospital wing uses commas correctly?
o: On July 4, 2026 the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas opened a new wing.
On July, 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
On July 4, 2026, the clinic in Austin, Texas, opened a new wing.
w: Two rules apply. In a full date, commas follow the day and the year when the sentence continues. In a city-state pair, commas follow the city and the state.

n.0: The comma after the year "2026" is missing.
n.1: The comma after the state "Texas" is missing.
n.2: No comma goes between the month and the day.

q: Which sentence confirming a patient's paperwork is punctuated correctly?
o: Ms. Chen, you finished, the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form, didn't you?
Ms. Chen, you finished the intake form didn't you?
Ms. Chen you finished the intake form, didn't you?
w: A name in direct address is set off by a comma, and a tag question (didn't you?) is also set off by a comma.

n.0: A comma must not separate the verb (finished) from its object, and the comma before the tag question is missing.
n.2: The comma before the tag question "didn't you" is missing.
n.3: The comma after the name in direct address is missing.

q: Which sentence using "however" contains a comma error?
o: However, the results were not available until Tuesday.
The results were not available until Tuesday, however.
The results were not available, however until Tuesday.
The results, however, were not available until Tuesday.
w: "However" used as an interrupter in the middle of a clause must be set off by commas on both sides: "available, however, until Tuesday". One comma is missing.

n.0: Correct: an introductory "However" is followed by a comma.
n.1: Correct: a closing "however" is preceded by a comma.
n.3: Correct: the interrupter is enclosed by a pair of commas.

q: Which sentence from a clinic's flu-season update needs a comma added?
o: Patients could visit on weekday evenings or on Saturday mornings.
When flu season began, the clinic extended its evening hours.
By March, waiting times at the clinic had dropped by half.
The clinic hired two nurses and the staff shared the extra shifts.
w: "The clinic hired two nurses" and "the staff shared the extra shifts" are independent clauses joined by "and," so a comma goes before "and." Without it, a reader first takes "two nurses and the staff" as one object.

n.0: This is one clause; "or" joins two phrases, so no comma is needed.
n.1: This sentence already has the comma after its introductory clause.
n.2: This sentence already has a comma after the introductory phrase "By March."

q: Which sentence about the night shift is punctuated correctly?
o: After the power failed, the nurses used flashlights, but the monitors, kept running.
After the power failed, the nurses used flashlights, but the monitors kept running.
After the power failed, the nurses, used flashlights, but the monitors kept running.
After the power failed, the nurses used flashlights but, the monitors kept running.
w: Two rules apply: a comma follows the introductory clause, and a comma goes before "but" when it joins two independent clauses.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject "the monitors" from its verb "kept."
n.2: A comma must not separate the subject "the nurses" from its verb "used."
n.3: The comma belongs before the coordinating conjunction "but," not after it.

q: Which sentence from a clinic door sign is punctuated correctly?
o: Patients who arrive after the doors close must use the side entrance.
Patients who arrive, after the doors close, must use the side entrance.
Patients, who arrive after the doors close, must use the side entrance.
Patients who arrive after the doors close, must use the side entrance.
w: "Who arrive after the doors close" is essential: it tells which patients must use the side entrance, so it takes no commas.

n.1: "After the doors close" is part of the essential clause, so it is not set off with commas.
n.2: Commas would make the clause nonessential, so the sign would tell every patient to use the side entrance.
n.3: A comma must not separate the long subject from its verb "must use."

q: Which sentence from a lab update is punctuated correctly?
o: The lab closed early the samples will be tested tomorrow.
Because the lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early; the samples will be tested tomorrow.
The lab closed early, the samples will be tested tomorrow.
w: A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

n.0: Two independent clauses with no punctuation between them form a run-on (fused) sentence.
n.1: "Because the lab closed early" is a dependent clause; a semicolon must join two independent clauses, so a comma belongs here.
n.3: Joining two independent clauses with only a comma creates a comma splice.

q: Which sentence about the patient's extra test is punctuated correctly?
o: The patient felt better; however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better, however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better; however the doctor ordered one more test.
w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

n.1: Commas on both sides of "however" leave two independent clauses joined by commas, a comma splice.
n.2: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.
n.3: The comma after "however" is missing.

q: Which sentence from an exam-day reminder uses the colon correctly?
o: The items to bring are: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring three items to the exam; your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring to the exam: your ID, your login, and a pen.
Bring three items to the exam: your ID, your login, and a pen.
w: A colon introduces a list only after a complete independent clause: "Bring three items to the exam" can stand alone.

n.0: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "are".
n.1: A semicolon does not introduce a list; it joins independent clauses or separates complex series items.
n.2: "Bring to the exam" is incomplete (the verb has no object), so it cannot introduce a list with a colon.

q: Which sentence listing a travel nurse's assignments is punctuated correctly?
o: Her assignments are in Boise, Idaho, Reno, Nevada, and Provo, Utah.
Her assignments are in Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
Her assignments are in Boise; Idaho, Reno; Nevada, and Provo; Utah.
Her assignments are in: Boise, Idaho; Reno, Nevada; and Provo, Utah.
w: When series items already contain commas (city, state), semicolons separate the items so each pair stays together.

n.0: With commas only, the reader cannot tell where one city-state pair ends and the next begins.
n.2: The semicolons are placed inside each pair instead of between the pairs.
n.3: A colon must not follow a preposition such as "in".

q: Which revision corrects the punctuation error? "The discharge packet includes: a medication list, a follow-up card, and a diet sheet."
o: Delete the colon after "includes"
Replace the colon with a semicolon
Move the colon to follow "packet"
Replace the colon with a comma
w: A colon must not separate a verb (includes) from its objects. Deleting it lets the list follow the verb directly.

n.1: A semicolon cannot introduce a list or separate a verb from its objects.
n.2: A colon after "packet" would split the subject from its verb, which is also an error.
n.3: A comma must not separate a verb from its objects.

q: Which sentence from a wellness poster uses a colon correctly?
o: One factor: mattered most to the team, getting enough sleep.
The factor that mattered most was: getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team; getting enough sleep.
One factor mattered most to the team: getting enough sleep.
w: A colon after a complete independent clause can introduce an explanation or example: "getting enough sleep" explains the factor.

n.0: A colon must not separate a subject (One factor) from its verb (mattered).
n.1: A colon must not come directly after a verb such as "was".
n.2: A semicolon must join two independent clauses; "getting enough sleep" is a phrase.

q: Which marks should enclose an interrupting phrase that already contains commas, to give it more emphasis than parentheses?
o: A pair of brackets
A pair of colons
A pair of semicolons
A pair of dashes
w: A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas or parentheses but gives more emphasis, and it can enclose an element that has its own internal commas.

n.0: Brackets mark the writer's own insertions inside a quotation.
n.1: A colon introduces a list, explanation or quotation after an independent clause; colons are not used in pairs.
n.2: Semicolons join independent clauses or separate complex series items; they do not enclose interrupters.

q: Which sentence pointing readers to an attached report uses parentheses correctly?
o: The results were normal. (see the attached report)
The results were normal (see the attached report.)
The results were normal, (see the attached report).
The results were normal (see the attached report).
w: When a parenthetical element ends a sentence but is not a full sentence of its own, the sentence's period goes outside the closing parenthesis.

n.0: A parenthetical that stands as its own sentence must begin with a capital letter and end with its own period inside the parenthesis.
n.1: The period belongs to the main sentence, so it goes outside the parenthesis.
n.2: No comma goes before an opening parenthesis.

q: A student quotes a nurse who said, "He refused the medication twice." The student wants to show that "He" means Mr. Diaz. Which version of the quotation is punctuated correctly?
o: "He (Mr. Diaz) refused the medication twice."
"He [Mr. Diaz] refused the medication twice."
"He, Mr. Diaz, refused the medication twice."
"He refused the medication twice [sic]."
w: Brackets mark words the writer inserts into someone else's quotation to clarify it.

n.0: Parentheses inside a quotation signal the speaker's own words, not the writer's insertion.
n.2: Commas would present "Mr. Diaz" as part of what the nurse said, changing the quotation.
n.3: [sic] marks an error in the original quotation; this quotation has no error and the name is still not added.

q: Which sentence about a wellness workshop uses hyphens correctly?
o: Twenty-one nurses joined the self care workshop this year.
Twenty one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the selfcare workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
w: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated, and the prefix self- always takes a hyphen (self-care).

n.0: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, and the compound modifies the noun "workshop".
n.1: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.
n.2: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, not closed up.

q: Which sentence describing a surgeon uses hyphens correctly?
o: The highly trained surgeon works a full-time schedule.
The highly-trained surgeon works a full-time schedule.
The highly-trained surgeon works a full time schedule.
The highly trained surgeon works a full time schedule.
w: Two rules apply. A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated (a full-time schedule), but no hyphen follows an adverb ending in -ly (highly trained).

n.1: An -ly adverb such as "highly" is not hyphenated to the word it modifies.
n.2: Both are wrong: "highly trained" takes no hyphen, and "full-time" before a noun needs one.
n.3: "Full-time" is a compound adjective before the noun "schedule", so it needs a hyphen.

q: A writer quotes "The vaccine, which was tested for two years, is safe for adults" but leaves out the middle clause. Which mark shows where words were removed?
o: An ellipsis
A pair of parentheses
A pair of brackets
A dash
w: An ellipsis (three periods) shows that words have been left out of a quotation: "The vaccine ... is safe for adults."

n.1: Parentheses enclose extra information; they do not show an omission.
n.2: Brackets mark words the writer adds to a quotation, not words taken out.
n.3: A dash marks a sudden break or adds emphasis; it does not show an omission.

q: Which sentence about a pediatric patient uses hyphens correctly?
o: The two-year-old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five-years-old.
The two-year-old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five years old.
The two-year old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five years old.
The two year old girl is in Room 4, and her brother is five years old.
w: A compound modifier before a noun takes hyphens (a two-year-old girl), but the same words after the noun do not (five years old).

n.0: "Five years old" follows the verb, not a noun, so it takes no hyphens.
n.2: Every word of the compound modifier is joined: "two-year-old," not "two-year old."
n.3: "Two-year-old" comes before the noun "girl," so it needs hyphens.

q: Which sentence about patients on a pediatric unit uses plural and possessive forms correctly?
o: The patients' in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patient's in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the childrens' toys.
The patients in Room 4 asked about the children's toys.
w: "Patients" is a plain plural subject, so it takes no apostrophe. "Children" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "children's".

n.0: The patients do not own anything here, so "patients'" (plural possessive) is wrong; the plain plural is needed.
n.1: "Patient's" uses an apostrophe to make a plain plural; plurals that show no ownership take no apostrophe.
n.2: "Children" already is plural; an irregular plural not ending in s takes 's, so "childrens'" is wrong.
